speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I quit because of what I am going to talk about today – second-hand smoke.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To be very honest, I did not quit for myself.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I quit because I knew that second-hand smoke will severely affect the health of my daughter.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I did not want her to suffer because of my choice to smoke.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The rights of smokers have to be protected.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They are adults, old enough to decide whether they want to smoke or not.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But we need to make sure that others are not affected by their decision to smoke.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Affected here is not just about not liking the smell of smoke or the discomfort of seeing the smoke.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: When I say affected, I mean you could die because of second-hand smoke.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Those inhaling second-hand smoke are actually exposed to more chemicals than the smokers themselves.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Sidestream smoke, the main component in second-hand smoke, is four times more toxic than the smoke that a smoker inhales from the cigarette.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am especially concerned about how second-hand smoke especially affects the vulnerable amongst us.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: According to MOH, even the slightest exposure to second-hand smoke can harm babies and young children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For them, even a little is already too much.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That is about one person dying every single day.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For years, many residents have reached out to me about their neighbours smoking at balconies and at windows.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second-hand smoke enters their homes, and they feel helpless about the health risks facing their families.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Chia shared how his baby cries whenever he inhales his neighbour's second-hand smoke.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Chia feels that he has tried everything.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He shut his window panels for most of the day and even installed a fan to blow the smoke away.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Yet, toxic fumes continue to enter into his home.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Her baby suffers from a lung infection and her neighbour smokes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She says, "He smokes at midnight and the second-hand smoke drifts into our room when we are sleeping soundly." How much more long-term damage will her baby suffer, she wonders.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Another resident, Ms Lam, lives with her elderly parents.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She often wakes up in the middle of the night to close the window so that her parents are not affected by her neighbours' second-hand smoke.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But this also means there is no ventilation in the home for fresh air.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They do not sleep properly and they are stressed out.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These are just some of the many concerns that residents have shared with me just over the past few weeks.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This increase was largely due to people smoking in or near homes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She said that her family started having eye and throat irritation, headaches and nausea during the circuit breaker period due to the prolonged exposure to second-hand smoke.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Her neighbour smokes seven to eight times a day, causing her to be "literally basked in a cloud of smoke" every day.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For Ms Lim and other Singaporeans, second-hand smoke is a silent assassin that poisons them in their own homes and they have no way to run.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Neighbours should try to solve problems by talking to each other – and they do try.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: When it does not work, they seek mediation and support from HDB, NEA, TC, RC, CMC, CDRT and Members of Parliament, a whole alphabet soup of authorities.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Yet, many residents have found these channels ineffective.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One such grievance was shared with me by Ms Ana.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She has suffered a second-hand smoke of a couple living below her unit for at least 10 years.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She has applied for CMC mediation, but her neighbours refused to attend the mediation, citing their right to smoke within their own home.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Similarly, her Members of Parliament have told her that they are "powerless" and "their hands are tied".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These stories highlight why talk is not enough.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: CMC mediation is voluntary and does not work when neighbours refuse to participate.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Even when Members of Parliament want to help, they cannot seek help from law enforcement because there is no relevant law or regulation to enforce.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The "neighbourly" issue of second-hand smoke is not the same as loud karaoke coming from next door or wet laundry dripping from upstairs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It cannot be solved the same way we solve all these other neighbourly disputes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This would minimise the effect that second-hand smoke has on their neighbours.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What is more, our proposal is very similar to what our NEA officers already do.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They issue advisories to residents, telling them, "not to smoke near the windows or at the balconies, as a way to minimise the amount of cigarette smoke emitted from their premises".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: All our proposal does is empower our officers to enforce their current advisory.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the past, NEA has also said that restricting people's actions in HDB flats would be an "intrusive regulatory approach".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, our law already intrudes on people's behaviour within their homes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We ban residents from being nude in their own homes if other people can see it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We ban residents from keeping cats in their own homes because we feel it might affect their neighbours.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Just this March, this House passed my Private Member's Bill, which bans the feeding of wildlife in any place, including private residences.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Why do we draw the line at nudity, pets and feeding wildlife, but not at second-hand smoke, something that kills hundreds of people in Singapore a year?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: After all, we do have existing laws that restrict someone from smoking in their car in the no smoking zone along Orchard Road if their windows are down.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: So, all our Government Parliamentary Committee or GPC asks for is to mirror these restrictions when it comes to our homes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Ultimately, our proposal seeks to balance the interests of both groups.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We allow smokers to smoke within their homes as long as they stay away from windows and balconies.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We allow non-smokers to avoid the perils of second-hand smoke.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We believe many other residents in HDB flats and private apartments would welcome such a restriction in their estates.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Last but not least, our proposal is enforceable using existing technology already used on the ground.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: NEA has been using cameras to catch high-rise litterbugs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These surveillance cameras are focused only on the external facade of the housing units being investigated to capture the act of littering.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These cameras can "detect objects in meeting high heat and capture images of the smoking offence".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: NEA can use all these existing technologies to catch those who smoke near windows and at balconies.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We have years of experience fine-tuning their use and to minimise privacy intrusion and to maximise successful enforcement.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What is missing now is just the legislation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If Minister's reply is that these technologies are not viable, then NEA should implement alternative solutions to facilitate enforcement.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: After all, when high-rise littering started killing people, we acted urgently to deploy solutions on the ground.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We must not let "hard to enforce" be an obstacle to saving lives Finally, I would like to share the experience of Mr Su, like me, a former smoker.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He shared with me that he used to enjoy sitting at his balcony with a coffee and cigarette, and his neighbours would respond by slamming their balcony doors and windows.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Su quit smoking after becoming a father.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But he now finds the tables have turned.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He is the one slamming the window now because he has neighbours who are now smokers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Belatedly, he realises the impact he has had on his neighbours.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We cannot afford to wait for smokers in Singapore to reach this same realisation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is a public health concern we cannot continue to deny and leave unresolved.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Many Members, including myself, have received similar suggestions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Indeed, I empathise with all who have suffered from this.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We have always recognised the serious health risk from second-hand smoke.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We first introduced smoking prohibition in omnibuses, cinemas and theatres in 1970 and have progressively expanded this to more public places.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We were among the first globally to impose a nation-wide smoking ban in the covered common areas of residential estates.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Singapore has introduced robust policies to discourage smoking, such as raising the minimum legal age of smoking and introducing standardised packaging for tobacco products.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Through public education and nudges, we urge smokers to quit their habit.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We continue to work on driving down smoking prevalence, which will also reduce the incidence of second-hand smoke.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: As more residents work from home during the COVID-19 pandemic, there has been an uptick in smoking complaints in residential estates.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Ninety-five percent or 6,310 of these complaints were related to smoking in common corridors, staircases and void decks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The remaining 5% or 320 cases involved smoking in homes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: NEA has prioritised surveillance at common areas, in particular, common corridors, staircases and void decks at residential estates.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Thermal cameras are also deployed at smoking hotspots.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: For complaints of smoking in homes, NEA, Town Councils and grassroots leaders take an educational approach and advise smokers to be considerate and not smoke near windows and balconies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Most smokers take heed, except for a small group of recalcitrant smokers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: For such cases, grassroots leaders, NEA and relevant agencies help to mediate between neighbours and discuss adjustments to be made.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Affected residents can turn to the Community Mediation Centre.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: They can also raise the matter to the Community Disputes Resolution Tribunal or CDRT as a last resort.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Quite a number of claimants were able to resolve issues amicably without proceeding to the Tribunal.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Mr Louis Ng and GPC Members have proposed that we ban smoking at balconies and windows of homes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We are just as keen to resolve this issue and have carefully studied these suggestions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Unfortunately, besides the fact that such legislation could be highly intrusive, there are significant practical challenges in enforcement that limit effectiveness.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: First, enforcement will be challenging as capturing evidence of the smoking offence is not straightforward.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Smelling the tobacco smoke is not sufficient as cameras must capture the smoker smoking or holding a lighted cigarette, as evidence for enforcement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: However, a smoker can easily hide behind a pillar, frosted glass windows, or curtains to avoid detection by the camera.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Overall, this may entail deployment of significant resources without achieving effective outcomes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Second, to capture the smoking act, the camera must be placed at suitable vantage points to probe into the window or balcony.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: For towering flats, finding the right vantage point in common areas to deploy the camera is not always possible.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Directly aiming cameras into homes is highly intrusive, unlike surveillance for high rise littering where the camera is trained at the building facade and can be placed at ground level some distance away.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: A dispute had ensued in 2017 between the condominium management committee and its residents when a circular directed residents to refrain from smoking at balconies and windows.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Some residents argued that the management committee should not dictate actions in private spaces.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We have studied overseas practices too, some of which were cited by the Member.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Globally, there are few instances of bans on smoking in homes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: In the US, the smoking ban in homes is limited to public rental housing which accounts for a tiny fraction, in fact, 1% of the total housing stock.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: In Australia, some states ban smoking in common areas of multi-unit housing and exempt private spaces, although owner corporations can adopt their own by-laws to cover the private living areas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Indeed, this is similar to what we have in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Smoking is already banned in many common areas of residential estates.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: MCSTs can opt to adopt by-laws to expand the ban in their estates, with support from residents.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: In US, the ban is enforced by Public Housing Authorities, whilst in Australia, the owner-corporations have to enforce the ban.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Even in countries where there are bans, effectiveness has been mixed and uncertain at best.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: In US public housing, there was difficulty in securing evidence for enforcement and smokers also saw this as a violation of privacy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The difficulties in enforcing against smoking in homes and privacy concerns can lead to greater frustration, exacerbate disputes and increase social tensions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: First, we will work harder to engender greater social responsibility.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This means instilling consideration for the health and well-being of those around us, not just family members but also our neighbours.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We must entrench new social norms of what constitutes acceptable behaviour.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: For example, stop smoking in homes, including at windows and balconies, and do so only in non-prohibited areas away from others.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: NEA will work with other agencies such as MOH, HPB and MND and MSO to explore effective ways of doing this.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: For example, by developing targeted messages on exercising social responsibility, as well as acceptable social norms.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: These can then be communicated pervasively across key platforms, including social media channels.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Changing norms will take time but we must work doubly hard as it gets to the very heart of the problem that legislation and enforcement, at least with today's level of technology, cannot fix.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: For example, we could develop simple messages for neighbours to communicate concerns with one another or share best practices from successful efforts to resolve neighbourly disputes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We will also look at how to leverage community networks and links, including grassroots, to bring neighbours together in conversations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Nonetheless, we hope that most cases will not have to end up in community mediation or with the Tribunal.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: And if they have to smoke, not to light up at home and instead smoke at non-prohibited areas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We are determined to address this and will work hard with Government agencies and the community on the strategies that I laid out.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: At the same time, we will continue to monitor best practices globally and improvements in technology.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We will stay open to innovative and practicable solutions as they emerge.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Ultimately, mitigating the impact of second-hand smoke requires everyone to play their part.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Smokers must exercise consideration for the health of their family and neighbours.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: As a community, we must help one another build the right social norms for a healthy and gracious society.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: The Adjournment does have 30 minutes, we have used 22 minutes of the 30 minutes.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: So, I will invite Members to ask clarifications and then the response has to be limited only to eight minutes up to 7.00 pm, which is the moment of interruption.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang: Thank you, Sir.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I was really hoping she would just said yes, but just two clarifications.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: One, I think the problem is that we are viewing this as a neighbourly dispute issue.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: If we view this as a public health crisis then the policy direction and the policy outcome might be completely different.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Two, I expected that we would raise the issue of whether it is enforceable and I addressed that in the speech that it can be.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Why can we not just use the cameras that we use for high-rise littering there is pointing at the facade of the building that can capture someone who is throwing a cigarette butt out of their window.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Why can we not use the same camera to capture someone smoking at their windows or the balconies and not point it inside to the house.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: So, if they are lying down on their bed and smoking, that is okay.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I am just saying move them away from the windows and balconies so that it minimises, not completely eradicate, but minimises the effects of second-hand smoke on the neighbours.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: To the Member's first question, we are dealing with this issue of second-hand smoke not just as a neighbourly dispute.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So, in fact, the smokers have very little areas, very little space for them to smoke.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: They cannot smoke in playgrounds, common corridors, staircases and so on.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In fact, somebody said, "Actually, our smoking prohibition in common areas in residential estate is really right up to the doorstep of your homes already." So, it is not really just about neighbourly disputes.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: But, as I have said to ban smoking in homes, there are couple of issues, not just about enforcement but also about privacy concerns.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So, that leads to my answer to the second question.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Why can we not just use the cameras we are using?

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Indeed, in my response, I have elaborated on why it is difficult to enforce using the cameras we have – both optical cameras as well as thermal cameras.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In fact, as the Member said, we have had years of experience using optical cameras for high-rise littering enforcement and then recently thermal cameras for enforcement against smoking in prohibited areas.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So, because we have years of experience, my NEA colleagues fully understand the intractable difficulties in enforcing against smoking at balconies and windows.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Allow me to just elaborate a little, Deputy Speaker.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: And as I have said, for high-rise littering, we can have the optical cameras at ground level point as Member said, at the facade, as long as you can see somebody throwing the cigarette – the act of throwing – we will then investigate from which floor, we know which unit, we can investigate and then get the person to admit to the littering offence.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For smoking at balconies and windows, as I have explained, it is not so easy because you need to see the smoker in the act of taking the lighted cigarette or holding the cigarette and to do that you have to train the camera at level with as well as directly at the windows or balconies.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: First, because of the design of flats and increasingly so, it is very difficult to find common areas where you can put cameras and be able to aim directly at that flat.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Flats, for instance, with recess windows and balconies, you cannot do it.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Most of the private condominium designs are very difficult, you cannot do it.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Even for high-rise littering, it is already difficult and that is just the facade.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For smoking, you actually have to look in.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: And the problem is, if you just step back behind, like I say, curtains, walls and so on, the person is actually still near the windows and balconies, but you cannot catch.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We have even thought about how do you do it if you cannot mount at the ground floor.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: You have to mount at a certain height and distance, but will you be able to find common staircases that there has a good vantage point?

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: If you cannot, can you mount it in the homes of residents?

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The other thing is, even for high-rise littering camera when you mount and aim, the camera will be looking at a few units, so there are actually privacy concerns.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: But for high-rise littering, because we are aiming at the facade, I think it is less of an issue.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: But, for smoking, it will be really an intrusion into privacy.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Because even the innocent resident may also be in the line of sight.
